warmup.q: Two programs that never stop computing share one CPU. You start one of them with nice -n 10, a command that marks a program as less important (0 is normal, and higher numbers mean "let the others go first"). About what share of the CPU does the less important program get?
options: About 50%: the setting only matters when the computer has nothing else to do
None: the normal program always goes first, as long as it has work
warmup.why: The kernel turns each nice value into a weight, nice 0 into 1024 and nice 10 into 110, and splits the CPU by weight: 110 out of 1,134 is 9.7%. In the lab box, the nice 10 loop got 0.98 s of CPU in 10 s. The third option is the tempting one, and the second section shows why Linux avoids it: a program that only runs when nobody else has work can wait forever. So Linux shares time out by weight, and the less important program gets less, never nothing.

sections.h: One CPU, two loops that never wait: the kernel has to choose
sections.html:
Let's start by counting. When this lesson was written, Docker's Linux system on the laptop had 12 CPUs and 1,055 tasks, counting every container. (The lab box is a small Linux machine that runs inside Docker. Docker is a program that runs such machines, called containers, side by side; on a Mac, they all share one hidden Linux system. A task is what the kernel calls a thread.) Only 9 of those tasks were ready to run. The rest were asleep, waiting for a network message, a key press or a timer.

The ready ones wait in a run queue, a list of tasks that want a CPU. Each CPU has its own. Every few milliseconds, for every CPU, the kernel answers one question: which task runs now, and for how long? The part of the kernel that answers it is the scheduler.

Picture one game console at home and three children who all want to play. Somebody has to decide whose turn it is. That's the scheduler's job, with tasks in place of children and a CPU in place of the console.

The simplest rule is to let a task run until it finishes or has to wait, then run the next one. It breaks as soon as one task never waits. Say the nightly job that adds up payments is a tight loop over a year of records. It never pauses for anything. On one CPU, every other task waits behind it until it ends, including the one that answers the card readers.

So the kernel must be able to take the CPU back from a task that won't give it up. The tool is the timer interrupt, from the first lesson of this track. It's a clock in the hardware that stops the CPU at a fixed rate and jumps into the kernel. On the lab box it fires 1,000 times a second, and each time the kernel may decide to run someone else. Saving one task's place (the values in the CPU's registers, its small working slots) and loading another's is a context switch.

With that, the next rule is round robin: each ready task gets a fixed time slice, say 3 ms, and then goes to the back of the line. At home, it's a kitchen timer next to the console. When it rings, the controller passes to the next child.

Let's watch it. spin.c is a small C program that loops without ever waiting, then reports how much CPU time it got. Two copies forced onto the same CPU split it evenly:

pid 19 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1866 times
pid 18 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1872 times

pid is the process id, the number the kernel gives each running program. Each copy was switched out about 1,870 times, so each turn lasted under 3 ms (4.99 s divided by 1,870 is 2.7 ms).

The length of the slice is a trade. A short slice gives a waiting task the CPU back sooner. But every switch costs a trip into the kernel, and the next task starts with the CPU's caches (small, fast memory on the chip) full of the last task's data. A long slice wastes less and makes everyone wait longer. With 3 ms slices and 30 busy tasks on one CPU, each task waits about 90 ms between turns.

Round robin's real flaw is that every task counts the same. The nightly totals job gets as much CPU as the program answering card taps, and there's nowhere to say that one matters less. Next, we'll give the kernel a way to hear that.

try.title: Two loops on one CPU
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box with docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. You get a shell (a window where you type commands) inside it. os/c/l04/spin.c loops for the number of seconds you give it, then prints the CPU time it got and how many times the kernel switched it out. gcc turns the C file into a program you can run.

taskset -c 0 runs a command on CPU 0 only, so the two copies have to share it. The & starts each copy in the background, and wait waits for both to end. Predict the split before you run the third line.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/spin os/c/l04/spin.c taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 5 taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 10 & taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 10 & wait

try.expect:
Process ids and switch counts differ between runs:

pid 17 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 5.00 s (100%), switched out 319 times
pid 19 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1866 times
pid 18 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1872 times

Alone, the loop gets the whole CPU. Its few hundred switches come from other work that landed on CPU 0 of Docker's hidden Linux system: other containers and the kernel's own tasks. Together, each copy gets half, in turns of about 2.7 ms.

sections.h: Nice values become weights, and a CPU is shared by weight
sections.html:
Back to the two loops. Say one of them is the nightly totals job and the other answers card taps. Round robin gives each half the CPU, and we'd like the totals job to step aside. Linux lets you say that a task matters less with its nice value, a number from -20 to 19. Higher means nicer to the others. Every process (one running program, with one or more threads) starts at 0. nice -n 10 cmd starts a command at 10, and renice changes one that's already running. Anyone can make their own process nicer. Making one less nice, which means more important, needs administrator rights by default (the CAP_SYS_NICE permission). Being kind is open to everyone; pushing to the front of the line takes permission.

The obvious design is strict priority: always run the task with the lowest nice value first. It starves. A nightly totals job at nice 10 would get no CPU at all while any nice 0 task had work, and on a busy computer that can be forever. Linux wants nice 10 to mean less CPU, never none.

So the kernel turns each nice value into a weight, from a fixed table in its source code:

nice -5 0 1 5 10 19
weight 3121 1024 820 335 110 15

When tasks compete for one CPU, each gets its weight divided by the sum of the weights. Nice 0 against nice 10 is 1024 / (1024 + 110): 90.3% against 9.7%. Each weight in the table is about 1.25 times the next one. The kernel's own comment says each nice level changes a task's CPU by about 10%, compared with a task that stays put.

Only the ratio matters. Nice 10 against nice 15 splits a CPU the same 75/25 way as nice 0 against nice 5. And a nice 19 task alone on an idle CPU still gets all of it. Weights only decide how to divide time among tasks that all want it at once.

How does the kernel hand out time by weight without keeping a record of every turn? It gives each task one number, its virtual runtime: the CPU time it has really had, scaled by 1024 divided by its weight. A nice 0 task's virtual clock runs at real speed. A nice 10 task's clock runs 9.3 times faster (1024 / 110), so 1 ms on the CPU adds 9.3 ms to it. The rule is then one line: run the task with the smallest virtual runtime. Heavy tasks (the ones with big weights) have slow clocks, stay behind, and get picked more often, exactly in proportion to their weights.

At home, picture a score sheet by the console that adds up each child's minutes, and the child with the smallest total plays next. If one child's minutes count nine times over, that child's turns come round far less often. The picture breaks when a child turns up late. With a score of zero, they'd play for an hour to catch up. The kernel never allows that: a task that starts late, or wakes from a long sleep, gets a virtual runtime close to the others' (Go deeper has the details).

That rule was the heart of CFS, the Completely Fair Scheduler, which Linux used from version 2.6.23 in 2007 until version 6.6 in 2023. The lab box agrees with the arithmetic. Nice 0 against nice 10 on one CPU:

pid 16 nice  0: 9.01 s of CPU in 10.00 s (90%), switched out 1381 times
pid 17 nice 10: 0.98 s of CPU in 10.00 s (10%), switched out 364 times

The shares come out right. The numbers say nothing yet about how long each task waits for its turn, though. Next, we'll see why that matters, and what replaced CFS.

try.title: Nice 0 against nice 10
steps: In the lab box, start one loop at nice 0 and one at nice 10, both on CPU 0. Predict the split from the weights 1024 and 110.
Halfway through, ps (a command that lists processes) shows each one's nice value in the NI column and its share of the CPU so far under %CPU.
Then change 10 to 5 and predict again.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/spin os/c/l04/spin.c taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 10 & taskset -c 0 nice -n 10 /tmp/spin 10 & sleep 5; ps -o pid,ni,pcpu,comm -C spin wait

try.expect:
PID  NI %CPU COMMAND
   16   0 89.8 spin
   17  10  9.5 spin
pid 16 nice  0: 9.01 s of CPU in 10.00 s (90%), switched out 1381 times
pid 17 nice 10: 0.98 s of CPU in 10.00 s (10%), switched out 364 times

That's 90.1% and 9.8%, against the 90.3% and 9.7% the weights predict. With nice 5, one run gave 7.53 s and 2.47 s: 75/25, as 1024 / (1024 + 335) says. The nice 0 loop's switch count moves a lot between runs, because other work on CPU 0 also switches it out. The nice 10 loop's count stays near 350.

sections.h: EEVDF: among tasks that are owed time, the earliest deadline runs
sections.html:
Smallest virtual runtime first gets the shares right, but it says nothing about when each task runs. Every task gets the same slice. Picture the program that answers card taps. It sleeps until a tap arrives, wakes up and needs 2 ms of CPU to answer. Under CFS, it could wait behind the totals job's full slice first, and a task had no way to say "I want short turns, often". CFS patched this with special rules for tasks that wake up.

Linux 6.6 began replacing CFS with EEVDF, short for Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First, and Linux 6.12 finished the move in 2024. The lab box runs 6.12. EEVDF keeps virtual runtime and adds two ideas, which its name hands us in order: eligible, then deadline.

The first idea is lag: how far a task is behind or ahead of its fair share. The kernel keeps a number called V, the average virtual runtime of all the ready tasks, in which heavier tasks count for more. V is where every task would be if the CPU had been shared perfectly. A task at or behind V has lag zero or more. It's owed CPU time, and it's eligible. A task ahead of V has had more than its share, and it waits, however urgent it looks.

The second idea is the virtual deadline. Each time a task starts a slice, the kernel sets it a deadline: the task's virtual runtime plus its slice, turned into virtual time (slice × 1024 / weight). Among the eligible tasks, the one with the earliest deadline runs. A task that asks for 1 ms slices gets an earlier deadline than one with 3 ms slices. So it runs sooner and more often, for less time each turn. Its share stays the same, and its waiting shrinks.

The default slice is 0.75 ms × (1 + log2 of the number of CPUs, counting at most 8). That's 0.75 × (1 + 3) = 3 ms on any machine with 8 or more CPUs, the lab box included. Since 6.12, a task can ask for its own slice with sched_setattr(), a system call (a request from a program to the kernel).

One result surprises people. A nice 10 task doesn't get shorter turns. It gets a full 3 ms slice every time it runs, but its deadline sits far ahead in virtual time, so its turns come rarely. In the nice 10 run of the last section, the loop ran 0.98 s in 364 turns: 2.7 ms each.

The stepper runs the first six slices for a nice 0 task and a nice 5 task, with the real numbers. Watch for the moment when the task with the earlier deadline still doesn't run.

Choosing well among tasks that compete is one job. A container needs something this choosing can't give it: a ceiling. Next, we'll see how the kernel builds one, and what it costs.

try.title: Read a task's turns from /proc
steps: /proc is a folder the kernel fills with live facts about every process. /proc/<pid>/schedstat holds three numbers for one task: nanoseconds (billionths of a second) on a CPU, nanoseconds spent ready but waiting in a run queue, and how many turns it got.

Start the nice 0 and nice 10 loops again, read both files after 5 s, and work out each loop's average turn: time on the CPU divided by turns. In the shell, $! holds the process id of the last command started in the background.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/spin os/c/l04/spin.c taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 6 & a=$! taskset -c 0 nice -n 10 /tmp/spin 6 & b=$! sleep 5 cat /proc/$a/schedstat /proc/$b/schedstat wait

try.expect:
4506153596 495090551 489
488818878 4507422520 190
pid 17 nice  0: 5.41 s of CPU in 6.00 s (90%), switched out 547 times
pid 18 nice 10: 0.59 s of CPU in 6.00 s (10%), switched out 225 times

The nice 10 loop ran 0.49 s in 190 turns, 2.6 ms per turn: about one 3 ms slice each time, as EEVDF promises. It spent 4.5 s waiting. The nice 0 loop averaged 9.2 ms per turn, often several slices in a row, because it stayed eligible with the earliest deadline. The middle number, time spent ready but waiting, is the one to watch when you suspect a CPU is overloaded.

sections.h: A CPU limit is a budget per 100 ms, and spending it early means a pause
sections.html:
Everything so far shares CPUs among tasks that compete for them. A container needs something else: a ceiling. Say a company rents one big computer and runs many containers on it. The payments program's container may use at most half a CPU, even when the computer is idle. Weights can't do that, because a task alone on a CPU gets 100% of it, whatever its weight.

So the kernel has a second tool. A cgroup (control group) is a group of processes that the kernel counts and limits together. In Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS, one capped how many threads a program could start. Every container is a cgroup. Its file cpu.max holds two numbers in microseconds (millionths of a second): a quota and a period. docker run --cpus=0.5 writes 50000 100000. The group may use 50 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms period. When the budget runs out, the kernel stops every thread in the group until the next period starts. That's throttling.

At home, it's a screen-time rule: 30 minutes an hour for the whole family, counted across every screen. If four children play on four tablets at once, the half hour is gone in seven and a half minutes. Then every screen stays locked until the hour turns, however idle the tablets are.

The budget is CPU time, not CPUs, and that's where the opening's pauses come from. Four busy threads on four CPUs spend 50 ms of CPU time in 12.5 ms of real time, then all four wait about 87 ms. To a card reader waiting for an answer, the program looks frozen. CpuQuota.java is a demo that runs busy threads and records every gap over 10 ms. Each gap is a moment when a thread wanted the CPU and didn't get it:

50000 100000
availableProcessors() = 1
4 busy threads for 2.1 s used 1.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 92, longest 94 ms
nr_periods 41
nr_throttled 40

The file cpu.stat counts what happened. nr_periods counts the periods that passed while the group had work, and nr_throttled the ones in which it ran out of budget: 40 of 41. A bigger limit doesn't change the shape. --cpus=2 with the same four threads gives a 200 ms budget, spent in 50 ms and followed by 50 ms of nothing. That run still saw 81 stalls, the longest 59 ms.

The JVM, the program that runs Java code, reads cpu.max when it starts and sizes itself from it. availableProcessors(), the Java method that reports how many CPUs a program may use, returned 1 under --cpus=0.5 (it rounds up) and 2 under --cpus=2. With one CPU, the JVM picks a simpler garbage collector, the part that frees memory a program no longer uses: Serial instead of the usual G1. It sizes its other thread pools from the same number. The quota never limits how many threads you start, though. Every extra busy thread spends the budget faster and makes the pause longer.

A CPU limit is a budget of time, not a number of CPUs. Count the threads that spend it.

There's a second way to give a container two CPUs. --cpuset-cpus=0,1 lets it run only on CPUs 0 and 1, with no budget at all. The same four threads got the same 4.0 s of CPU, and only 2 stalls over 10 ms. The comparison below has both runs.

Kubernetes, a program that big companies use to run containers across many computers, sets CPU limits the same way as Docker. Its documentation says "cpu limits are enforced by CPU throttling".

One question the scheduler never asks is what a task is doing when its turn ends. Next, we'll see why that matters when two threads need the same data.

try.title: Throttle a Java program with a CPU limit
steps: This one runs from the labs folder on your Mac, not in the lab box. Each command starts a fresh container with a CPU limit, prints its cpu.max, compiles the demo with javac (the Java compiler), runs it and prints the throttling counters.
Predict how much CPU time four busy threads get in 2 s under --cpus=0.5, and how long the longest pause is.
Run it, then run it again with --cpus=2 in place of --cpus=0.5.

code.title: on your Mac, in labs/
code.html: docker run --rm --cpus=0.5 -v "$PWD":/labs -w /labs sfz-labbox:1 bash -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l04/demo/CpuQuota.java java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l04.demo.CpuQuota 4 2 grep -E "nr_(periods|throttled)" /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat'

50000 100000
availableProcessors() = 1
4 busy threads for 2.1 s used 1.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 92, longest 94 ms

nr_throttled 40

Half a CPU's worth of time: 1.0 s in 2 s. The longest stall is close to a whole period, because the four threads spend the 50 ms budget early and then wait out the rest. The counters include the periods javac used before the demo started. With --cpus=2 you should see 200000 100000, availableProcessors() = 2, 4.0 s of CPU and still dozens of stalls (81 in one run, the longest 59 ms).

aside.title: Why doesn't the CPU graph show the pauses?
aside.html: A graph of CPU use usually shows an average, often over 10 seconds or a minute. A throttled thread uses no CPU while it waits, so its pause adds nothing to the graph. A program with a limit of 2 CPUs can average 1.2 and look comfortable, while every busy moment ends in a pause of tens of milliseconds. The counters in cpu.stat don't average anything away. If nr_throttled climbs along with nr_periods, the limit is the cause.

opening:
Picture the computer behind the café's card readers. One program answers each tap of a card; another adds up the day's payments. Both are made of threads, sequences of steps that run side by side. The computer has a few CPUs, the parts of the chip that run them, one thread at a time each.

Then the payments program moves into a container, a fenced-off corner of a shared computer, limited to half a CPU. Most answers take a few milliseconds. A few take almost 100 ms, on a computer that's mostly idle.

It's easy to read "half a CPU" as half speed, like a car in a low gear; the setting's name invites it. The kernel, the core of the operating system, enforces it as bursts and pauses.

In Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS, every thread became a task the kernel runs. In this lesson, we'll see how the kernel picks the next task, how a lower priority shrinks a share without starving it, and where those pauses come from. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a payments program that paused for almost 100 ms on an idle computer. Its limit of half a CPU was a budget of 50 ms per 100 ms, and four busy threads spent it in 12.5 ms, then waited out the rest of each period.

On a Mac, open Activity Monitor and look at the bottom of its CPU tab: it counts the threads your computer is running right now. Compare that number with your CPUs, and remember that the scheduler is sharing them out every few milliseconds.

Next, we'll let two threads change the same balance at once, and see how a lock makes one of them wait without wasting its turn.

compare.title: Two CPUs' worth of time, or two whole CPUs, with four busy threads

a.label: --cpus=2 (a quota)
a.title: CpuQuota 4 2
a.html:
200000 100000
availableProcessors() = 2
4 busy threads for 2.0 s used 4.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 81, longest 59 ms
nr_periods 25
nr_throttled 22

b.label: --cpuset-cpus=0,1 (a CPU set)
b.title: CpuQuota 4 2
b.html:
max 100000
availableProcessors() = 2
4 busy threads for 2.0 s used 4.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 2, longest 13 ms
nr_periods 0
nr_throttled 0

compare.note: Both containers got 4.0 s of CPU in 2 s, and the JVM saw 2 processors in both. The quota let all four threads run at once on four CPUs. They spent each period's 200 ms in 50 ms, then sat throttled for the other 50. The CPU set gave no budget, only two CPUs, so the scheduler shared them among the four threads in 3 ms slices, and nobody waited more than a few slices. Same total, very different worst case. For a program people wait on, like the one answering card taps, the worst case is what they feel.

worked.title: Find out whether a program's pauses come from its CPU limit

steps.say: Read the budget from inside the container. The file holds two numbers in microseconds: the quota, then the period. max in place of the quota means no limit.
steps.code: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max # 200000 100000 -> 200 ms of CPU time every 100 ms: a limit of 2 CPUs

steps.say: While real traffic runs, read the counters twice, ten seconds apart. Subtract to get how many periods passed and how many of them ran out of budget. The ratio of the two is the share of periods in which the group was throttled.
steps.code: grep -E 'nr_(periods|throttled)' /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat; sleep 10 grep -E 'nr_(periods|throttled)' /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat # nr_periods 25 / nr_throttled 22 in the --cpus=2 demo: throttled in 88% of periods

steps.say: Check what the JVM believes, because it sizes its thread pools from this. The flag -XshowSettings:system prints the container settings the JVM found.
steps.code: java -XshowSettings:system -version 2>&1 | head -6 # Operating System Metrics: # Provider: cgroupv2 # Effective CPU Count: 1 # CPU Period: 100000us # CPU Quota: 50000us

steps.say: Count the threads that want a CPU at the same moment. ps -L prints one line per thread, and an R in its stat column means running or ready to run. If that count is well above the quota in CPUs, each period's budget goes in a fraction of the period. Fix it by cutting busy threads (smaller pools, or fewer garbage-collector threads with -XX:ParallelGCThreads) or by raising the limit. Then read cpu.stat again to confirm that nr_throttled has stopped climbing.
steps.code: ps -L -p $pid -o tid,stat,pcpu,comm | awk '$2 ~ /^R/' | wc -l

lab.title: Build a small scheduler: round robin, weighted fair and EEVDF
steps: Open spin-nice.txt. It's real output of this lesson's spin.c from the lab box: three pairs of loops on one CPU, at nice 0 against 10, 5 and 0. The tests compare your simulator with these numbers.

Read Scheduler.kt from top to bottom. The weight table, Task, Timeline and Cpu.run are written for you. Cpu.run is a pretend CPU: it asks the scheduler for a task, runs it for sliceFor(task) ms, calls charge so the scheduler can update its numbers, and repeats.
Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All eight fail for now.
Write WeightedFair.pick and charge. The test that compares with the lab box should now pass: 90/10, 75/25 and 50/50.

Write Eevdf.eligible, pick and charge. The stepper's order, A B A A A B, is one of the tests. The last test shows a task with a 1 ms slice waiting at most 3 ms for its turn, while still getting only a third of the CPU.
hints: tasks[next++ % tasks.size] is a whole round robin: % wraps the count back round to the first task.
minBy returns the first of several equal smallest values, which is the tie-break the tests expect.
EEVDF's pick is filter then minBy. The filtered list is never empty: the task with the smallest virtual runtime is always at or behind the weighted average.
In Eevdf.charge, compare with a little slack (task.vruntime >= task.deadline - 1e-9). Computers store fractions slightly inexactly, so 3.0 can come out as 2.9999999999999996.

drill.title: Weights, virtual time and the EEVDF pick, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the three lines at the heart of EEVDF: how a task's virtual runtime grows, which tasks are eligible, and which eligible task runs. Then write what cpu.max holds after --cpus=0.5, and what its two numbers mean.

answer.html: // after a task runs ms of real time task.vruntime += ms * 1024 / task.weight // nice 0 = 1024, nice 10 = 110 // eligible: owed time, at or behind the weighted average V val v = tasks.sumOf { it.weight * it.vruntime } / tasks.sumOf { it.weight } val eligible = tasks.filter { it.vruntime <= v } // earliest virtual deadline wins; deadline = vruntime + slice * 1024 / weight val next = eligible.minBy { it.deadline } // --cpus=0.5 -> /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max = "50000 100000": 50 ms of CPU time per 100 ms

recap: The scheduler is the part of the kernel that picks which ready task runs on each CPU, and for how long. A timer interrupt lets it take the CPU back, and a context switch hands the CPU to the next task.
A nice value, from -20 to 19, becomes a weight (nice 0 is 1024, nice 10 is 110). Tasks that compete for a CPU share it by weight, so nice 0 against nice 10 is 90/10, and nobody is starved.
Virtual runtime is real CPU time × 1024 / weight. EEVDF, Linux's scheduler since 6.6, runs the eligible task (one at or behind the weighted average V) with the earliest virtual deadline.
The default slice is 3 ms on 8 or more CPUs. A shorter slice makes a task wait less between turns without giving it more CPU. /proc/<pid>/schedstat shows time on the CPU, time waiting and turns.

cpu.max is a budget, not a CPU count: 50000 100000 is 50 ms of CPU time per 100 ms. Busy threads spend it early, and the whole group pauses until the next period; cpu.stat counts those periods in nr_throttled.
The limit: the scheduler shares out time, but it never asks what a task is doing when its turn ends. If that task holds something another thread needs, the other thread waits too.

explain.prompt: A friend runs the café's payments program in a container with a limit of 2 CPUs. They say: "The graph says we average 1.2 CPUs, so CPU can't be why some payments take 60 ms longer." Explain what the limit really is, and how it can still be the cause.
explain.answer: The limit isn't two CPUs. It's a budget in cpu.max: 200 ms of CPU time every 100 ms period, shared by every thread in the container. The computer underneath has many CPUs, so in a burst of payments ten threads can run at once on ten CPUs and spend the whole 200 ms in about 20 ms. Then the kernel throttles the container. No thread runs until the next period starts, up to 80 ms later, and any payment in the middle waits. The graph averages over many periods, and a paused thread uses no CPU, so the average still looks comfortable. The proof is in cpu.stat: if nr_throttled climbs along with nr_periods, the limit is biting. To fix it, make fewer threads compute at the same moment, for example with smaller thread pools, or raise the limit.

deeper.html:
Schedulers you can load. Linux 6.12 also added sched_ext, a way to write a scheduling policy as BPF programs (small programs the kernel checks for safety and then runs inside itself) and load it while the computer runs. If the loaded scheduler misbehaves or leaves a task waiting too long, the kernel drops it and moves every task back to EEVDF. You can't try it in the lab box, because Docker Desktop's kernel is built without it:

$ zcat /proc/config.gz | grep SCHED_CLASS_EXT
# CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT is not set

On a Linux kernel built with it, /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state says whether a BPF scheduler is loaded, and the kernel's source code has example schedulers such as scx_simple in its tools/sched_ext folder.

Groups come before tasks. The fair scheduler weighs groups as well as tasks. Every cgroup has a cpu.weight (100 by default, from 1 to 10000). CPU time is first divided among sibling groups by their weights, then among the tasks inside each group by nice. That's why nice doesn't cross container boundaries: a nice 19 loop in one container and a nice 0 loop in another split a CPU by the containers' weights. A Linux desktop does the same for terminal windows, through a feature called autogrouping. Each terminal session gets its own group, so two loops started from two different terminals ignore each other's nice values. /proc/sys/kernel/sched_autogroup_enabled is 1 in the lab box too.

Tasks that sleep. This lesson's loops never sleep, but most real tasks do. In CFS, a task that had slept for a long time came back with a small virtual runtime and could hold the CPU for a while, so CFS moved waking tasks forward to near the smallest virtual runtime. EEVDF handles it with lag. A task that goes to sleep stays in the run queue for a while (the kernel docs call it "deferred dequeue"), and its lag decays, so a long sleeper comes back with its lag reset.

Pressure across the whole machine. PSI, pressure stall information, measures waiting for many tasks at once: /proc/pressure/cpu for the whole machine, and cpu.pressure in each cgroup. In the lab box the first one read some avg10=5.78: over the last 10 seconds, at least one task was waiting for a CPU 5.78% of the time. That's run-queue waiting, the same thing the middle number of schedstat measures for one task.

Requests and limits in Kubernetes. Kubernetes lets each container ask for two things about CPU. A request decides which computer the container is placed on and becomes its cpu.weight. A limit becomes its cpu.max. Teams that need steady response times often set a request and no limit, or a limit well above their busiest moment, and keep the number of threads that compute at once close to their budget.
